notes.text: The final unit of the named chapter records Rav Ilish’s description of the manner of carrying a Passover offering.
Yuchasin supplies the opening report. Gittin describes common captivity and Ilish’s conditional intention to bring them back, before their response deters him.
The named Rav Naḥman’s article records both the captive daughters and the exact chapter.
Gittin’s exact narrative introduces the daughters and says that Rav Ilish was captured with them.
Mal 8 is the specific article. The Arukh gives the account while expounding a gloss it cites from Rabbenu Ḥananel.
The checked Arukh directly supports both parts of Heilprin’s quotation, with minor wording differences.
The passage explicitly introduces an unnamed man as knowing bird language and gives him the interpretive replies.
Rashi identifies Ilish as the person addressing the interpreter.
Ilish rejects the raven, then treats the dove as an omen. The unnamed man gives the same repeated words in each exchange.
The comparison of Israel to a dove motivates the stated expectation of a miracle.
Rashi identifies both fugitives and explicitly qualifies the unnamed man as the interpreter.
Ilish reached safety across the water; the other man was found and killed.
Heilprin’s inference is grounded in the narrative’s express assignment of knowledge to the interpreter. Retain it as Heilprin’s conclusion alongside the contrary accounts.
The Tartu witness corroborates the attribution to Ilish and the rescue attempt that Heilprin disputes.
Rava expressly calls Ilish a great man in the discussion of a contract left to his sons.
Rava rebukes Ilish with the judges-of-Ḥatzatzta wording. Rashbam identifies Ilish as the embarrassed party.
The Bavli quotes Isaiah 60:22 after Ilish’s embarrassment.
Ilish raises the marital property objection and Rava is the embarrassed party here, as Rashi’s discussion confirms.
Ilish explicitly asks Rava about sending a slave with a borrowed cow.
Heilprin explicitly quotes the kabbalistic report under Rav Naḥman. The checked source prints Bela in parentheses and Bera in brackets.
The source’s הוא תיקון identifies a kabbalistic relationship. The received Heilprin wording Bela is preserved, with the Bera variant registered separately.
The base Arukh article was checked. The alleged lack of a correction in Musaf HeArukh still requires direct comparison with a separately identified supplement edition.
